speaker: Rory Sutherland
title: Marketing Expert: The Playbook Behind Every Great Campaign | Rory Sutherland
question: In customer-facing service industries, why does improving operational reliability metrics often fail to improve brand perception?
guest: Royal Mail couldn't make any sense of the fact that their brand perception bore no relation to service levels. There were districts where every single first-class letter arrived early the following day—extraordinarily reliable service—and Royal Mail wasn't particularly held in affection or esteem. There were other areas where the service was frankly a bit ropey and people seemed to love it. They put a theory to the test and proved it right: the major determinant of whether you liked Royal Mail was whether you liked your postman. People with unreliable service whose postman did the odd favor, left things in the porch, or had a chat thought it was a brilliant organization regardless of the operational metrics. In any service organization—an electricity, gas, or water utility—you may interact online ninety-five percent of the time, but the one or two occasions where you interact by telephone or face-to-face disproportionately affect your perception. If every personal experience is a good one, in the human brain that's a good organization you can trust. We don't have evolved experience in evaluating postal efficiency; we have half a million years of evolved experience deciding who to like and trust, so we use human judgment as a proxy.

points.core: Customers lack intuitive ways to evaluate abstract operational reliability metrics.
points.note: Accept: humans have no evolved or direct intuition for judging aggregate delivery rates, SLAs, or backend operational efficiency. Do not credit: generic claims that customers do not read reports or do not care about reliability.

points.core: Buyers substitute rare personal interactions as a trust proxy for organizations.
points.note: Accept: judging an entire company by whether they like and trust a frontline human representative (such as a delivery worker or support agent). Do not credit: generic praise for good customer service without the proxy-evaluation mechanism.

points.core: A single warm human encounter disproportionately outweighs routine automated transactions.
points.note: Accept: rare phone or face-to-face interactions dominating brand perception despite 95%+ of interactions being routine digital or self-service touchpoints. Do not credit: vague statements that customer experience matters.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Because reliability is mostly a "hygiene factor": customers expect it, so delivering it prevents dissatisfaction but rarely creates delight. In Kano-model terms, on-time performance or uptime is a must-have attribute whose absence damages perception sharply, but whose presence earns little credit. That asymmetry is compounded by several things.

First, perception is built from memorable moments, not averages. People judge experiences by peaks and endings, and a single vivid failure (a stranded flight, a botched outage response) outweighs hundreds of uneventful successes. Negative events also spread further through word of mouth and media.

Second, internal metrics often measure what the company controls, not what the customer feels. A flight can be "on time" by padded schedules, or a call "resolved" by the system's definition, while the customer still found the experience stressful or indifferent.

Third, brand perception lags and is sticky. Reputations rest on accumulated stories and prior beliefs, so incremental improvements go unnoticed unless they cross a perceptible threshold or are communicated.

Finally, perception is driven heavily by how staff handle problems: empathy, communication, and recovery, which reliability metrics do not capture.

points.why: The response describes reliability as expected and internal metrics as misaligned with customer experience, but does not explain that customers lack an intuitive way to judge aggregate reliability.
The response credits staff empathy and recovery with shaping perception without explaining that customers use trust in a frontline employee as a proxy for trust in the organization.
The response explains how a vivid failure can outweigh routine successes but never connects that disproportionate effect to a rare, warm human encounter.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer: Improving operational reliability often fails to lift brand perception because customers judge services through subjective, emotional experiences rather than system-wide averages. Reliability functions primarily as a baseline expectation rather than a differentiator: failures spark frustration and erode trust, whereas flawless execution largely goes unnoticed. Moreover, internal metrics typically track isolated touchpoints or aggregate averages, such as overall uptime or mean wait times, masking the painful tail-end disruptions and fragmented end-to-end journeys that individual customers actually endure. Even when operations run smoothly, human memory follows the peak-end rule, weighting emotional warmth, perceived fairness, and empathetic service recovery far more heavily than routine mechanical precision; a punctual interaction that feels cold or rigid rarely builds brand affinity. Finally, brand perception is sticky and shaped by confirmation bias. Once customers associate a company with poor service, they selectively remember occasional glitches while discounting quiet operational gains, meaning behind-the-scenes improvements seldom shift sentiment unless paired with visible, human-centered changes in how the brand communicates and treats people.

points.why: The response says aggregate metrics can hide individual disruptions but does not explain that customers lack an intuitive way to judge aggregate reliability.
The response values warmth and empathy but does not say customers use their trust in a frontline representative to judge the whole organization.

The response gives emotional warmth more weight than mechanical precision but does not establish that a rare personal encounter can outweigh many routine automated transactions in shaping brand perception.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Improving operational reliability often doesn't improve brand perception because customers treat reliability as the minimum, not as a reason to like a brand. In the Kano model it's a "must-be" attribute. In SERVQUAL terms, it keeps you inside customers' zone of tolerance. Failures cause anger, but doing it right just meets expectations, so raising on-time rates from 92% to 96% mostly prevents complaints rather than creating delight.

Several other effects add to this. When things go right, nothing happens, so customers don't notice or remember it. Negative events count far more than positive ones, and by the peak-end rule people judge experiences by their worst and final moments rather than averages. Perceptions also lag reality: reputations built on past failures, reviews and word of mouth take years to change.

There's also a measurement gap. Internal metrics like uptime, average handle time or on-time departure measure what the company controls, not what customers live through. Averages hide the bad tail experiences that drive stories, and a flight can depart on time while the overall trip is still miserable.

Finally, brand perception is shaped more by emotional and relational moments, like empathy, recovery after failures, personalization and fairness, than by efficiency. Reliability protects the brand, but those human moments are what build it.

points.why: The response identifies a gap between internal metrics and lived experience without explaining that customers lack an intuitive way to judge aggregate reliability.
The response says relational moments shape brand perception without explaining that customers infer the organization's trustworthiness from a frontline representative.
The response gives human moments more weight than efficiency in general without explaining how one rare, warm encounter can outweigh many routine digital transactions.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
Improving operational reliability often fails to lift brand perception because customers treat reliability as a baseline expectation rather than a differentiator. It acts like a hygiene factor: falling short triggers sharp frustration, while incremental gains above an acceptable threshold go largely unnoticed because people rarely register problems that never happen.

There is also a gap between how companies measure performance and how customers experience it. Operational metrics track averages like uptime or on-time rates, whereas perception is shaped by negativity bias and emotional peaks. Raising on-time performance from 93% to 97% looks impressive on a dashboard, yet a single stressful delay or indifferent recovery can still define a customer's impression. Meanwhile, as service improves, expectations quietly reset upward, erasing any lasting delight.

Ultimately, brand perception responds less to silent consistency than to visible cues like empathy, communication, distinctiveness, and grace under pressure. Reliability protects a brand's floor, but it rarely raises its ceiling.

points.why: The response explains why reliability gains go unnoticed once expectations are met but never claims customers lack an intuitive way to judge aggregate reliability.
The response mentions empathy and communication without explaining that customers infer an organization’s trustworthiness from a frontline representative.
The response says a stressful delay or indifferent recovery can define an impression but never claims that a rare warm human encounter outweighs routine automated transactions.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Improving operational reliability often fails to improve brand perception because companies measure how consistently a process runs, while customers judge how well the service meets their expectations. An airline can improve its on-time departure rate, for example, while passengers still miss connections or struggle to get help when plans change. The metric improves, but the experience that shapes their opinion stays the same.

Reliability is also often a baseline expectation. Customers take routine success for granted, while a single disruptive failure can stand out, especially if the company communicates poorly or makes the customer do the work of fixing it. Brand perception tends to shift when improvements are noticeable, address problems customers care about, and happen consistently enough to change what customers expect from the company.

points.why: The response describes a mismatch between what companies measure and what customers value without explaining why customers lack an intuitive way to judge aggregate reliability.
The response mentions difficulty getting help but does not explain how customers use trust in a frontline worker to judge the whole organization.
The response explains why a disruptive failure stands out against routine success but does not identify the outsized effect of a warm personal encounter amid routine automated transactions.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Operational reliability metrics track what the company delivers. Brand perception reflects what customers notice, what they expected, and how the experience made them feel. A hotel can cut room-readiness delays in half, yet most guests see little change because their rooms were already ready when they arrived. They also take a ready room for granted. For the guest whose room is late, an unexplained wait or a dismissive response can leave a stronger impression than several trouble-free stays.

Reliability gains are more likely to change brand perception when they solve a problem customers care about and customers experience the difference often enough to revise their expectations.

points.why: The hotel example explains why guests may overlook a reliability gain, leaving their ability to intuitively evaluate aggregate reliability metrics unaddressed.
The candidate says a dismissive response can leave a strong impression but does not describe customers using trust in a frontline representative to judge the organization.
The candidate explains how a bad experience can outweigh several trouble-free stays but does not show how a rare warm human encounter can outweigh routine automated transactions.
